items.title: The Impact of AI Applications on Smart Decision-Making in Smart Cities: The Mediating Roles of the Internet of Things and Smart Governance
items.abstract: Smart cities increasingly depend on digital technologies to manage urban services, use resources efficiently, and respond to the changing needs of citizens. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help city authorities analyse complex information, predict future conditions, and make informed decisions. However, the success of AI-based systems depends on more than their analytical capabilities. They also require reliable data from the Internet of Things (IoT) and governance practices that ensure transparency, accountability, and responsible use of technology. This paper examines how AI applications may influence smart decision-making in smart cities, with particular attention to the mediating roles of IoT integration and smart governance. Recent research published between 2024 and 2026 is reviewed to understand developments in AI-enabled urban services, connected infrastructure, and responsible digital governance. Based on this review, an integrated conceptual framework is proposed to explain the relationships among AI applications, IoT integration, smart governance, and decision-making outcomes. The framework considers decision accuracy, responsiveness, transparency, and resource efficiency as important dimensions of effective urban decision-making. It also highlights challenges related to data quality, privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, and public trust. Eight research hypotheses and a quantitative research methodology are proposed for future empirical investigation. The paper contributes a structured basis for examining how technological capabilities and governance arrangements may work together to support better urban decisions. The proposed relationships require validation through data collection and statistical analysis

items.title: The Impact of Digital Technology Adoption on Employee Engagement: A Qualitative Approach
items.abstract: The rapid uptake of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has changed the way work is carried out in organizations, bringing with it together new opportunity and new challenges for employee engagement. This approach looks at the effects of the approval of digital technology on employee engagement, with an exact focus on the organization's use of AI, the application of AI in sustainable Human Resource Management (HRM), employee trust and how often GenAI is used. In order to carry out the study, a qualitative multiple-case study method is used, based on four studies that had been published earlier and which were carried out in different organizational settings. The results show that AI adoption leads to superior levels of employee engagement if the technologies provide clear benefits related to employees' work, are compatible with the organization's current processes, and are properly supported by top management. By helping employees develop their skills, motivate them and grant them with opportunities to contribute, sustainable HRM practices implemented with AI can also help to further increase employee engagement. Trust among employees is also identified as a critical factor; as positive attitudes to AI are connected to superior levels of organizational commitment, which is positively related to employee engagement. Furthermore, while larger usage of GenAI does not necessarily correlate with greater job satisfaction, there is several evidences to propose that an increase in usage can lead to increased work engagement. The study findings indicate that the acceptance of digital technology is more than just about the technology being available: it relies on the responsible deployment, on the training of employees, on the enhancement of digital literacy, on the transparency of communication and on the support and engagement of leadership. Overall, the results emphasize the significance of a multi-faceted approach, encompassing both technological innovation and employee well-being and sustainable HRM practices, to foster authentic employee engagement and ensure the long-term effectiveness of the organization.

items.title: The impact of hazards on health of crew members under implementation of bunker operations and substantiation of complex of measures on development of security system
items.abstract: The bunkering of vessel is mandatory and technologically complex stage of organization of maritime transportation, associated with high level of occupational health risk for the crew members of both receiving and bunkering vessels. During bunkering operations, at sampling ship fuel, as well as work inside fuel tanks, the crew is exposed to complex impact of toxic vapors and aerosols of petroleum products. This exposure can result in development of acute pathological states and formation of chronic occupational diseases affecting respiratory, nervous, cardiovascular systems as well as haematopoiesis organs.In order to elaborate recommendations to decrease negative health aftermaths for health of crew members under bunkering operations, comprehensive analysis of organizational technological aspects of bunkering was carried out. It permitted to identify key irregularities regarding the stated subject and to formulate recommendations for their elimination.

items.title: The impact of schoolbag weight and carrying style on musculoskeletal pain: A 5-year prospective cohort study among schoolchildren in Misrata, Libya
items.abstract: Background: Musculoskeletal pain is a growing public health concern among school-aged children, with significant physical and psychosocial implications. Schoolbag weight and carrying style have been identified as critical ergonomic risk factors. However, evidence from developing countries, including Libya, remains limited, particularly regarding longitudinal impacts. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the association between schoolbag weight, carrying style, and musculoskeletal pain over a five-year period among elementary schoolchildren in Misrata, Libya. Methods: A cohort of 443 elementary schoolchildren (grades 1-4) was followed for five years, with 421 completing all assessments. Data were collected on schoolbag weight, carrying style, walking duration, and pain characteristics. Descriptive statistics, Chi-square tests, and logistic regression were applied to explore the prevalence and predictors of pain. Repeated Measures ANOVA and Friedman tests were used to assess changes in continuous and categorical outcomes across time points. Results: Musculoskeletal pain prevalence increased from 0.0% at baseline to 10.1% at the first follow-up before declining to 5.6% and 6.2% in subsequent follow-ups. Carrying style emerged as the most significant predictor of pain, with the mid-back (T12) style reducing the risk of pain by up to 98.8% compared to the low-back (L3) style. Schoolbag weight, while exceeding recommended thresholds, was not a significant predictor of pain. Gender differences were noted, with girls at higher risk during early follow-ups. Walking duration played a marginal role, influencing pain risk only in the first follow-up. Conclusion: This study highlights the critical role of ergonomic carrying styles, particularly the mid-back (T12) position, in reducing musculoskeletal pain among schoolchildren. Findings challenge the conventional emphasis on bag weight alone and highlight the need for multifaceted interventions, including ergonomic education and policy changes, to promote musculoskeletal health.

items.title: The Impact of the Generative AI Implementation Environment on Employees’ Intention to Adopt, Mediated by Psychological Variables
items.abstract: This study aims to empirically investigate the structural pathways through which organizational factors associated with the adoption environment of generative artificial intelligence (AI) influence employees' intentions to adopt AI through psychological mechanisms.Based on the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, a macro-level technology adoption model, the adoption environment was categorized into technological, organizational, and environmental factors.AI self-efficacy and AI anxiety were established as mediating variables representing opposing psychological mechanisms, while intention to adopt was specified as the dependent variable.To empirically test the proposed research model, a survey was conducted among 327 Korean employees who were currently using generative AI in their work.The hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling (SEM) and bootstrapping analysis.The results indicate that both technological and organizational factors significantly enhanced AI self-efficacy while simultaneously reducing AI anxiety.Environmental factors had a significant positive effect on AI self-efficacy but did not have a significant effect on reducing AI anxiety.Furthermore, AI self-efficacy was found to have a positive effect on intention to adopt, whereas AI anxiety was identified as a key mediating factor that negatively affects intention to adopt.This study contributes to the literature by identifying an integrated mechanism through which macro-level environmental stimuli are translated into behavioral intentions through individuals' internal psychological evaluations.From a practical perspective, the findings suggest that organizations should move beyond simply following external trends in generative AI adoption.Instead, they should focus on enhancing employees' self-efficacy through technological maturity and internal organizational training, while simultaneously addressing employees' concerns and fears regarding potential technological replacement.

items.title: The Importance of Cybersecurity for Business Leaders
items.abstract: This chapter establishes why cybersecurity is now a core business leadership responsibility rather than a purely technical function. It examines the fundamental drivers behind escalating cyber risk, including human behavior, rapid technological advancement, imperfect software design, artificial intelligence, geopolitical instability, and the commoditization of digital capability. The chapter explains why traditional technology-centric approaches to cybersecurity frequently fail and why business alignment, governance, resilience, and executive engagement are critical to success. The discussion highlights the economic realities of cybersecurity, including the impossibility of achieving perfect protection, the limitations of compliance-based thinking, and the operational challenges of defending organizations in a continuous 24/7 threat environment. It also explores how security, safety, and trust increasingly influence customer value propositions and competitive differentiation. The chapter concludes by presenting a strategic vision for cybersecurity that integrates business objectives, organizational resilience, risk management, and leadership accountability into a practical executive framework for decision-making in the age of AI.

items.title: The Influence of N. M. Suetin on the Work of Artists at the Leningrad Porcelain Factory
items.abstract: This study examines the influence of the artistic and pedagogical legacy of Nikolai Mikhailovich Suetin – chief artist of the Leningrad Porcelain Factory – on the work of the factory’s sculptors and artists.The stylistic impact of N. M. Suetin's supremacist works on the individual creativity of the factory's artists is traced on a specific material, and the phenomenon of the art laboratory, which he directed, is revealed. The work of his students and colleagues contemporary to N. M. Suetin is highlighted, as well as the legacy of his ideas, which continued to live in the artistic porcelain of the LFZ of the second half of the 20th century. When considering the products of the LFZ, the models of artistic porcelain were mainly selected, which are subject to further mass replication. The choice of mass–produced objects is determined by the basic principles of creating artistic porcelain, developed by N. M. Suetin himself - the priority of rational, ergonomic and utilitarian product design, while preserving the perception of the object as a work of art. The result of the work was the identification of a rarely mentioned in the art history literature connection of the professional activity of N. M. Suetin with the formation of the original school of artistic porcelain of LFZ.

items.title: The making of cloud computing: an antecedent of scalability
items.abstract: This paper offers a historically situated analysis of cloud computing. Cloud computing is a paradigm for provisioning computing infrastructure that now has enormous reach. It is defined by its unique scalability. This unique scalability has proven to be enormously impactful in the digital economy and beyond, shaping the emergence of platform ecosystems, the development of AI, and the process of digitalization in the 21st century. As important as it is to grapple with this scalability, it is easy to reify. This paper examines emergent sociotechnical practices that sought to make the computer more flexible. The study focuses on specific efforts within the Research Department of a major US technology company. The analysis of scalability I offer is based on interviews with former engineers in this Lab as well as archival material. I trace projects and practices as teams forayed into making a relatively fixed machine more dynamic and more scalable. This paper advances emerging literatures on cloud computing and digital infrastructure by offering a grounded analysis of scalability-in-the-making.

items.title: The mediating role of job crafting in the relationship between perceived organizational support and nurses' attitudes towards artificial intelligence: a cross-sectional study based on the job demands–resources model
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is being rapidly integrated into clinical nursing, yet many nurses remain ambivalent or resistant to these technologies. While perceived organizational support (POS) and job crafting have each been linked to nurses’ work attitudes, little is known about how they jointly shape nurses' views on AI. Drawing on the job demands–resources (JD-R) model, in which perceived organizational support represents a job resource and job crafting a proactive behaviour, this study examined whether job crafting mediates the association between POS and nurses' attitudes towards AI application. Methods Between April and June 2026, 314 clinical nurses from a tertiary grade A hospital in China were invited via convenience sampling; 305 returned valid responses. Participants completed the Perceived Organizational Support Scale (POSS), the Nurse Job Crafting Scale (NJCS), and the Chinese version of the Attitudes towards AI Application at Work (AAAW) scale; items 14–21 of the AAAW were reverse-scored. Mediation was tested using the SPSS PROCESS macro (Model 4) with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results Mean item scores were 3.86 (SD = 0.80) for POS, 3.90 (SD = 0.59) for job crafting, and 3.46 (SD = 0.68) for AI attitudes. All three variables showed significant positive correlations (r = 0.502–0.715, all p < 0.01). Job crafting partially mediated the POS–AI attitudes relationship, accounting for 60.8% of the total effect (indirect effect = 0.248, 95% CI [0.169, 0.337]). The direct effect of POS remained significant after controlling for the mediator (b = 0.160, p = 0.006). Because AAAW is multidimensional, the model was also tested on theoretically distinct facets; the indirect effect was significant for positive perceptions (0.301, 95% CI [0.203, 0.403]) but not for AI-related concerns. Conclusions Job crafting was associated with the relationship between POS and nurses’ AI attitudes in a pattern consistent with partial mediation. Organizational support and job crafting were associated with more positive attitudes toward AI, consistent with the JD-R model. Both factors may matter for AI adoption in nursing. The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these pathways.

items.title: The Non-Perceiving Listener: A Naturalistic Mixed-Methods Study of University Students' Self-Directed Help-Seeking from Large Language Models
items.abstract: This pre-registration outlines a 36-month PhD research programme investigating how university students in China seek psychological support from Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world, self-directed settings. The study addresses a critical gap in the literature: existing evidence is dominated by controlled, simulation-based experiments, which fail to capture how students actually disclose distress (indirectly, gradually, and culturally framed) in naturalistic environments. The research comprises three integrated components: Component 1 (Naturalistic Interaction): A prospective observational study of 100–150 students who use their own chosen LLM for a personal concern. Data includes pre/post questionnaires (PHQ-9, GAD-7, help-seeking attitudes), transcripts (with consent), and a coding module assessing crisis response, therapeutic technique (MITI), and cultural responsiveness. Component 2 (Written Responses): A structured open-ended qualitative instrument administered to all Component 1 participants to explore the mechanisms behind model choice, disclosure decisions, and crisis boundaries. Component 3 (Governance Feasibility): A Delphi consensus process and comparative case studies (4 universities) to identify feasible institutional governance mechanisms for LLM integration in counselling services. Key Hypotheses/Propositions: Students will select models based on availability and privacy, not clinical evidence. Naturalistic disclosure will be more indirect and culturally framed than controlled benchmarks. Safety failures (e.g., missed indirect risk) will be more frequent in naturalistic use than simulation studies suggest. Governance standards will be feasible only when implemented at the system level, not prompt level. Timeline: The study is planned for 36 months (proposed start: September 2027). Data collection has not yet commenced and is contingent on institutional ethics approval. Registration Type: OSF Preregistration (Standard). This registration covers the design, sampling, and analysis plan prior to any data collection.

items.title: The Prediction Optimization Bridge (POB): A Surrogate Assisted Random Forest–NSGA-II Framework for Energy Efficient Vehicle Routing
items.abstract: Urban freight transport is an essential component of urban mobility, playing a key role in supporting the economic and social development of cities. However, the growth of freight and delivery activities can intensify energy consumption and increase pressure on urban transportation systems. In this context, the Energy-Efficient Vehicle Routing Problem (EE-VRP) has emerged as an important research challenge, requiring a balance between routing complexity and non-linear operational dynamics. From this perspective, data-driven and intelligent optimization approaches can support more efficient decision-making in urban transportation systems by integrating operational efficiency with energy performance. To address this challenge, this paper proposes the Prediction-Optimization Bridge (POB) model, a hybrid Artificial Intelligence and Multi-Objective Optimization framework that seamlessly integrates supervised machine learning with multi-objective evolutionary optimization. The proposed model combines a Random Forest surrogate model with the NSGA-II evolutionary algorithm to identify efficient vehicle routes. First, we used the RF surrogate to capture complex non-linear relationships and minimize total fleet energy consumption. Then, the predicted energy values are subsequently integrated into the NSGA-II multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, which explores alternative routing solutions. To enhance operational realism, a dynamic payload updating mechanism adjusts vehicle load after each delivery, reflecting the progressive reduction in transported goods along the route. As a result, the Random Forest surrogate achieved a predictive accuracy of R2 = 0.9960. Furthermore, the proposed framework attained an average energy reduction of 12.47% ± 2.32% compared with a conventional distance-greedy routing heuristic, while achieving a normalized Hypervolume of 0.6305 ± 0.0277 over five independent experimental runs. Feature importance analysis based on Gini metrics identified vehicle load as the most influential factor affecting energy consumption (approximately 70%). Overall, the results demonstrate that integrating vectorized machine learning surrogates with evolutionary multi-objective optimization provides an efficient, robust, and reproducible approach for developing energy-efficient and sustainable fleet routing strategies.

items.title: The principle of humanitarization as a methodological basis for implementing the discipline “Technologies of personal growth and social interactions” at a university
items.abstract: The goal of the research is to theoretically substantiate the principle of humanitarization as a system-forming methodological foundation for implementing the universal discipline “Technologies of personal growth and social interactions” at a higher education institution. The empirical basis of the study consisted of the curricula of Russian universities on the relevant topic, their comparative analysis, as well as the experience of the Siberian Federal University in teaching this course, its pedagogical analysis and generalization. The article substantiates the relevance of this course, describes and pedagogically interprets the experience of the Siberian Federal University in teaching students the technologies of personal growth and social interactions from the standpoint of humanitarization and digitalization of education. The scientific novelty of the research lies in summarizing and presenting the experience of implementing this course at different universities in the form of a classification of teaching models for the discipline in question, with a characterization of their didactic potential and the risks of reducing personal development. Specifically, the lecture-academic (theoretical), training-coaching (practice-oriented), and integrative-blended models have been identified. The latter compensates for the shortcomings and enhances the advantages of the first two models (theoretical training in the mode of synchronous lecture-webinars is complemented by practice-oriented training conducted at in-person seminars, and pedagogically justified, predominantly asynchronous independent work of students in the university’s information and educational environment). As a result of the study, prospects for the development of the course have been formulated in the context of the humanistic paradigm and digital transformation. These include pedagogically justified integration of artificial intelligence into education while preserving reflection, the “end-to-end” implementation of electronic portfolio technology in the educational process at the university, and the development of inclusive and ethical components of the discipline content.

items.title: The psychophysics of affect in large language models
items.abstract: Good decisions often require considering how outcomes will feel. Yet large language models (LLMs) increasingly enter decision workflows, despite little being known about how they map outcomes to feelings or use those mappings in choice. We tested how LLMs anticipated gambling or stock-trading outcomes would feel and whether they incorporated these ratings into choice. When outcomes were rated in isolation, ratings exhibited diminishing sensitivity to magnitude, resembling human value functions; but models rated gains more intensely than equivalent losses, an inversion of canonical loss aversion we call silicon gain amplification. When outcomes were rated together, enabling direct comparison, ratings linearised. In choice, the gain-loss asymmetry largely disappeared, and models' own ratings did not reliably explain their choices better than monetary utility did. These findings reveal malleable mappings from outcomes to affect, raising questions about whether and how agentic LLMs should incorporate anticipated feelings into decisions.

items.title: The Relationships among Intrinsic Motivation, Work Engagement, and Job Burnout among Female Beauty Professionals
items.abstract: This study examined the relationships among intrinsic motivation, work engagement, and job burnout among female beauty professionals, who account for the large majority of the Korean beauty service workforce. Data from 233 respondents were analyzed using SPSS Statistics 27.0. Intrinsic motivation comprised autonomy and competence, work engagement comprised dedication and absorption, and job burnout comprised reduced personal accomplishment and depersonalization. Autonomy and competence both predicted dedication, whereas only competence predicted absorption. Autonomy and dedication reduced both dimensions of burnout, while competence and absorption were associated with higher burnout; since neither showed a significant bivariate correlation with burnout, these coefficients are interpreted as suppression effects that emerge once autonomy and dedication are controlled. These findings indicate that intrinsic motivation does not function as a uniformly protective resource. Discretion over one’s work and a sense of meaning buffer burnout, whereas competence and sustained absorption may impose psychological costs unless workload and recovery time are managed. Beauty service organizations therefore need to expand autonomy and support competency development while regulating workload at the same time. Given the limited explanatory power of the burnout models, future research should incorporate job demands and organizational resources.

items.title: THE ROLE OF TECHNOLOGY IN HUMANITIES EDUCATON AND FUTURE DEVELOPMENT TRENDS
items.abstract: Humanities education is a fundamental field that shapes an individual’s spiritual, cultural, and moral values. In the era of globalization and digital transformation, this field is undergoing significant changes, enriched by innovative technologies and new teaching approaches. As a teacher, I observe that modern technologies not only make lessons more engaging but also enhance students’ critical thinking and independent learning skills.Interactive learning platforms, digital libraries, virtual tours, multimedia tools, and artificial intelligence are increasingly integrated into humanities education. For instance, in literature classes, students can go beyond traditional reading by analyzing texts through digital tools, participating in discussions, and creating their own interpretations. This approach fosters creativity, analytical thinking, and communication skills. At the same time, the role of the teacher is evolving. The teacher becomes a mentor, facilitator, and motivator rather than just a source of information.Technology supports teachers by making the educational process more efficient, accessible, and engaging.

items.title: The Silvopastoral Systems in Latin America: A Systematic Review of Productive, Environmental Impacts and Adoption Factors in Sustainable Livestock Production
items.abstract: Livestock production supports food security, employment, and rural development in Latin America, while conventional extensive grazing systems can contribute to soil degradation, biodiversity loss, deforestation, and greenhouse gas emissions. Silvopastoral systems (SPS), which integrate trees, shrubs, forage species, and livestock, offer an approach to addressing these environmental pressures alongside production objectives. This study aimed to examine the evolution of SPS research, productive performance, environmental contributions, and sociotechnical factors influencing adoption in Latin America. A systematic literature review with qualitative evidence synthesis was conducted using scientific publications indexed in academic databases and published between 2014 and 2025. The synthesis examined reported productive and environmental outcomes alongside the economic, institutional, and cultural conditions shaping implementation. The reviewed studies reported improvements in forage quality, animal nutrition, productive efficiency, animal welfare, and soil fertility. Environmental benefits included biodiversity conservation and contributions to climate change mitigation through carbon sequestration and reduced greenhouse gas emissions. The literature also showed a shift from predominantly ecological and productive assessments toward broader sociotechnical perspectives incorporating institutional arrangements, economic conditions, and cultural practices. Despite these documented benefits, adoption remained constrained by limited access to financing, inadequate technical assistance, weak public policies, and reluctance to modify established production practices. These findings highlight the importance of connecting technical knowledge with the conditions under which producers make management decisions. The review concludes that scaling SPS requires coordination among producers, researchers, institutions, and policymakers, supported by accessible financing, sustained technical assistance, and effective public policies. By integrating evidence on production, environmental outcomes, and adoption, the study provides a basis for designing strategies responsive to local conditions and advancing sustainable livestock production across Latin America.

items.title: The social reality of precarity: sex work, gender and migrant labour in Thailand and Malaysia
items.abstract: Purpose This article examines how state regulation, migration governance and informal labour markets intersect to produce precarious labour in Thailand and Malaysia, with focused attention on gendered and migrant dimensions, especially sex work. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual article draws on peer-reviewed academic literature, policy documents and international organisation reports. The conceptual framework is developed through synthesis of these sources, applying Richard Quinney's (1970) six-proposition theory of the social reality of crime to examine the mechanisms through which labour precarity is produced and reproduced. Findings Precarious labour is produced through six interconnected mechanisms that parallel Quinney's propositions. The analysis reveals that formal labour protections coexist with, and are systemically undermined by, enforcement gaps, corruption, deliberate production of illegality and media-driven stigmatisation. Migrant workers, sex workers and transgender individuals experience extreme precariousness where these mechanisms intersect. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual article, the findings require empirical testing through further research with precarious workers themselves. Practical implications Meaningful policy responses must address all six precarity-producing mechanisms comprehensively, including migration reform and challenging stigmatising discourses. Social implications The article reframes precarious labour as a socially produced phenomenon rather than an economic inevitability, exposing how legal exclusion, enforcement practices and stigmatising discourses systematically marginalise vulnerable workers. It calls for societal recognition that these patterns are sustained by design and neglect, requiring a shift in how labour vulnerability is understood and addressed across Thailand and Malaysia. Originality/value The article extends Quinney's six-proposition criminological framework to labour precarity, developing the social reality of precarity model that proposes precarity is actively produced through governance rather than existing merely as an economic condition. This article illustrates how governance mechanisms operate interdependently to generate, sustain and reproduce labour vulnerability across distinct national contexts.

items.title: The STEAM Governance Framework: A Simple Five-Phase Operating Cycle for Organizational Clarity, True Conformity, and Sustainable Continuity (Standardize, Train, Enforce, Assess/Reassess, Maintain)
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Organizations across every sector frequently suffer from an operational condition best described as acceptable chaos: a state in which teams sit through repetitive status meetings, juggle conflicting spreadsheets, and generate constant activity without shared definitions, enforceable standards, or lasting results. Existing process and project methodologies often make this problem worse either by introducing heavy ceremonial overhead (such as mandatory daily standup meetings that pull staff away from real work to recite tasks managers should already know) or by treating governance as a static policy binder that is written once and quietly ignored. To solve this breakdown at its root, independent systems architect and researcher Josie O. Magee Bélanger created the STEAM Governance Framework within JosieVerse Enterprise (JVE). Built on the core operational rule to always be proactive to avoid being reactive, STEAM organizes governance into five sequential and continuously self-correcting phases: (S)tandardize: Establish an authoritative Standards Guidebook, one shared vocabulary, clear Pass/Fail readiness criteria, and a Single-Source Digital Database that eliminates spreadsheet-based tracking. (T)rain: Establish role-specific training requirements and practical, easy-to-follow playbooks that align every participant to the shared standard before enforcement begins. (E)nforce: Uphold top-down accountability across all ranks (ending "do as I say, not as I do" exceptions), apply transparent Pass/Fail decision gates with time-bounded executive risk-acceptance waivers when exceptions are necessary, report gaps honestly, and publicly commend full compliance. (A)ssess / Reassess: Conduct recurring end-to-end audits, capture structured Lessons Learned, and maintain a Live Executive Dashboard for 24/7 proactive awareness, routing any drift back to Standardize, Train, or Enforce through the Diagnostic Calibration Loop. (M)aintain: Sustain long-term institutional memory and staying power through a predictable communications and outreach plan, a standing cross-functional working group of unit points of contact (POCs), continual process improvement, and subject-matter expert (SME) continuity libraries. This whitepaper establishes the canonical public definition of the STEAM Governance Framework, traces its roots in the natural cycle of growth and order across families, field units, and enterprises, illustrates its impact through a composite enterprise vignette, presents the 5 Ws and How behind its design, compares STEAM with established industry frameworks, separates the Live Executive Dashboard from the Four-Quadrant Executive Decision Brief, outlines ten practical governance principles, and explains why STEAM is built to govern the coming Human+AI (H+AI) workplace. items.title: The trap of appearing perfect: When servant leaders accidentally intensify follower over-commitment and workaholism
items.abstract: Can striving to look perfect backfire when your leader puts you first? We examine this question through the concept of perfectionistic self-presentation (PSP), an impression management (IM) motivation to appear flawless to others. Drawing on IM theory, we argue that employees high in PSP may feel compelled to appear flawless to their leaders, increasing their tendency to overcommit to them as salient evaluative audiences and, in turn, have higher workaholism. We also propose that servant leadership, a leadership style that emphasizes serving and cultivating followers, amplifies the relationship between followers’ PSP and overcommitment to leaders. Across three time-lagged field studies, two conducted in China and one in the United Kingdom, we find that individuals high in PSP are more likely to report workaholism through overcommitment to the leader, particularly when reporting to servant leaders. Our findings show how a normally positive form of leadership can have unintended costs when interpreted through followers’ self-presentational motives, extending understanding of PSP, IM, and the boundary conditions of positive leadership.

items.title: The unforeseen tradeoff: could AI scribes alter the cognitive and relational work of clinical documentation?
items.abstract: AI scribes can reduce the documentation burden and allow clinicians to spend more face time with patients. However, we propose a hypothesis-generating concern that by reducing the active cognitive work of composing clinical notes, AI scribes may alter the encoding of patient encounter details into memory, particularly the narrative and relational details, as distinct from the informational content already captured in the chart. Our viewpoint advances a theoretically grounded hypothesis based on clinical observations and existing literature directly or indirectly relevant to clinical documentation, warranting future empirical investigation. The proposed tradeoff is most relevant to longitudinal care and may vary with documentation workflow and clinician experience. Because relational continuity and clinician recall may be important to the doctor-patient relationship, the shift toward AI-generated notes therefore raises questions about how to preserve meaningful cognitive engagement while benefiting from reliable clinical records.

items.title: The use of artificial intelligence by academic teachers in Poland
items.abstract: Objectives The study examines the attitudes of Polish academic teachers toward the use of artificial intelligence in teaching and research, with particular emphasis on their experiences, perceived benefits and concerns. Material and methods The research was based on a quantitative survey conducted in the first half of 2025 using an online questionnaire distributed to public and private universities in Poland. A total of 560 academic teachers participated in the study. The survey explored the scope of AI use in teaching and research, self-assessed competences, perceived advantages and risks, willingness to participate in training, and opinions on institutional regulations concerning AI. Results Most respondents declared experience with AI in teaching rather then research, with younger academics being more likely to use such tools. AI was mainly used for creating teaching materials, searching literature, translating texts, editing content, and preparing tests. Respondents identified time savings, reduced language barriers, and support for creativity as the main benefits of AI. Non-users most often pointed to lack of need, distrust of generated content and ethical concerns. Most respondents had not participated in formal AI training, although expressed willingness to attend such courses. Conclusions The findings suggest that AI is becoming an increasingly important element of academic work in Poland, particularly as a tool supporting repetitive and time-consuming tasks. However, its broader implementation remains limited by insufficient competences, ethical concerns, legal uncertainties, and distrust of AI-generated content.

items.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-SUPPORTED DECISION SYSTEMS IN STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT IN HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS
items.abstract: This study examines, through a conceptual and literature-based approach, how strategic management processes in higher education institutions can be transformed by artificial intelligence (AI)-supported decision systems. AI applications that can be used in the strategic analysis, strategy formulation, implementation, and monitoring-evaluation stages are mapped onto one another, and the resulting synthesis is presented in tables. The findings indicate that AI-supported decision systems have the potential to improve the quality of strategic decisions in areas such as predicting student success and enrollment, resource allocation, quality assurance, and environmental scanning. However, data quality, algorithmic bias, transparency, ethics and governance, institutional capacity, and academic autonomy emerge as critical challenges. The study proposes a human-centered hybrid decision model and a five-stage implementation roadmap. It concludes that AI should be positioned in higher education management not as a substitute for human decision makers but as a tool that strengthens their strategic judgment.

items.title: The use of generative artificial intelligence in the creation of supplemental learning materials in higher education
items.abstract: This exploratory cross-sectional study examined undergraduate public health students’ perceptions and attitudes of supplemental interactive books created with H5P Smart Import, a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tool designed to accelerate the development of learning materials. Guided by the Successive Approximation Model), interactive books were developed for an online undergraduate public health course at a large public university in Texas. The study analysed survey data from the second semester of a larger three-semester instructional design project. During the study semester, students used supplemental interactive books created with GenAI; half were subsequently revised and enhanced by the instructor, while the remaining were used in their artificial intelligence (AI)-generated form. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to examine students’ perceptions, acceptance ratings, and preferences regarding the interactive learning materials. Overall, 72% of students reported positive perceptions of the interactive books. A paired-samples t-test indicated that instructor-enhanced interactive books received significantly higher acceptance ratings than AI-generated-only books. Findings suggest that GenAI tools, such as H5P Smart Import, may support efficient development of instructional materials, but instructor review and enhancement may improve student acceptance. Future research should examine how prompt design influences the quality of GenAI-generated materials and should use larger samples and explanatory mixed-method designs to better understand student experiences.

items.title: The use of theories, models and frameworks to institutionalise routine data-driven decision-making in sub-Saharan African health facilities: a scoping review
items.abstract: Abstract Background Limited use of routine data for decision-making plagues Sub-Saharan African (SSA) health facilities despite key investments in health system data infrastructure to harness routine health-data. Evidence remains limited on how theories, models, and frameworks (TMFs) guide, inform, and assess efforts to institutionalise routine data-driven decision-making in SSA health facilities. This review aimed to determine which TMFs have been used to institutionalise routine data-driven decision-making in SSA health facilities and examine how they have been applied. Methods We searched six databases (MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, Global Health, and CINAHL). Publications on data use in SSA health facilities were included. Extracted data included year of publication, study location, study design and intervention type. We conducted framework analysis to assess TMFs use in strengthening data use for decision-making in SSA health facilities. Results 44 papers (Qualitative = 23, quantitative = 7, mixed methods = 14) published between 2007 and 2025 across fourteen SSA countries were included. The fourteen identified TMFs for institutionalising routine data-driven decision-making were mostly determinant frameworks (29/44, 65.9%) which explored behavioural, technical and organisational data use factors. Few studies explained factor interaction over time to institutionalise data use. Common reported decision forums were performance monitoring (n = 13/44) and data/audit review (n = 7/44) meetings with 10/44 studies having unspecified decision-making forums. When featured, routine data use was operational (logistics, service delivery monitoring, target setting). Conclusion Determinant frameworks dominated the TMFs evidence-base of efforts to institutionalise routine data-driven decision-making and seldom explained their interaction over time. Institutionalisation requires understanding routine data use as a dynamic sociotechnical process where technologies, workflows, organisational structures and human behaviours interact over time. Routine data use across SSA health facilities remains operational rather than integrated into strategic and clinical decision-making. There’s need for systems thinking to identify better ways to leverage TMFs to strengthen routine data-driven decision-making eco-systems in SSA health facilities.

items.title: The work of assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Drawing on Walter Benjamin’s concept of aura, this chapter reconceptualises current debates about university assessment in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) as struggles over the place of auratic educational practices. It argues that AI does not simply threaten assessment security or academic integrity, but destabilises the historical connection between assessment and the authentic, situated and original performance of student work. Against both techno-solutionism and nostalgic returns to restrictive assessment ritual, the chapter proposes a more discriminating account of when auratic practices remain educationally justified. Its central claim is that aura matters most where it preserves forms of friction that are intrinsic to learning, including effort, uncertainty, error, frustration, and self-doubt. On this basis, the chapter argues that the key task for assessment design is not merely to defend human originality as such, but to distinguish between arbitrary constraints and those conditions of authentic performance that substantively support learning and student self-realisation.

items.title: Threat Alerting System for Surveillance Camera Using Ensemble Model
items.abstract: The fusion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Computer Vision into video surveillance is critical when it comes to managing public safety and resources. Traditional research has been based on simple motion sensors or manual monitoring which is not allowing massive video streams to be interpreted effectively. Consequently, security operations require in real-time automated solutions for the identification of the particular threat instead of analysing these through the methods of reactive forensics. This research presents an intelligent video analysis framework with the use of a hybrid Deep Learning architecture. Instead of processing simple 2d images the study makes use of the UCF-Crime data set of detecting realistic anomalies that include a static threat (for example weapons) with dynamic temporal (for example fighting/robbery). These inputs are similar to the standard CCTV, presenting the ability of the intelligent systems to assist decision making for security operations. To check this ability to detect complex threat, in the paper a combined methodology of CNN, YOLO and Inflated 3D ConvNets (I3D) is implemented. The research takes into account various scenarios and it uses YOLO for “object detection” and I3D for “action recognition” to determine performance, to identify the optimum configuration. Furthermore, the research solves practical problems, such as balancing the processing speed (FPS) and high level of accuracy in order to reduce false alarms as much as possible. Experimental results prove the superiority of the proposed automated Threat Alerting System that combines object detection and spatio-temporal analysis. Ultimately, this framework will encourage situational awareness, remove human error and to ensure proactive public safety.

items.title: Three-dimensional models of the multiple myeloma bone microenvironment: from disease mechanisms to translational applications
items.abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a hematological malignancy strongly dependent on the bone microenvironment (BME), a dynamic niche that supports malignant plasma cell (PC) survival, immune escape, bone disease, and drug resistance. Conventional two-dimensional (2D) cultures and animal models have provided important insights into MM biology, but they only partially reproduce the spatial organization, cellular complexity, extracellular matrix composition, mechanical cues, and soluble gradients of the human bone marrow (BM). Three-dimensional (3D) models have therefore emerged as complementary experimental platforms to investigate microenvironment-dependent mechanisms of disease progression, therapeutic resistance, and patient-specific drug response. In this review, we provide a critical assessment of both bone-specific and BM like 3D models of MM, with a particular focus on their ability to recapitulate key functional aspects of tumor-bone microenvironment interactions and myeloma bone disease. We differentiate systems that mainly mimic the general BM niche from those that incorporate bone-relevant features, and we evaluate the available platforms based on the biological mechanisms they reproduce, the functional readouts they enable, and their suitability for distinct experimental and therapeutic purposes. We also highlight their relevance for therapeutic target validation and drug testing using patient samples. Finally, we discuss how the integration of patient-derived cells, spatial technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI) may enhance the interpretability and translational value of 3D MM models, ultimately supporting the development of more microenvironment-driven therapeutic approaches.

items.title: TokWatt: an open, boundary-annotated database of AI inference energy, from chat answers to agents
items.abstract: Electricity supply is becoming a binding constraint on the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI), yet public evidence on the energy used by a single AI task is scattered and hard to compare. Published figures for one chatbot answer differ by two orders of magnitude, largely because studies count different parts of the system and measure different units of work. We present TokWatt, an open database of 134 published estimates of AI inference energy drawn from 13 sources (2023-2026) and covering 20 tasks, from classic machine-learning inferences to chat answers, reasoning answers, long-document queries, image and video generation, and coding agents. Each estimate records its functional unit, five measurement-boundary components, method, reported interval, and the location of the value in its source. A reproducible procedure scales estimates to a common server-plus-facility boundary and derives per-task reference values with ranges. The reference values span six orders of magnitude: 0.34 Wh for a short chat answer (range 0.16-0.99 Wh), 4.7 Wh for a reasoning answer, 124 Wh for a short video clip, and 150 Wh for one task delegated to a coding agent. Five independent estimates for default production chat systems agree within a factor of 1.8, and the reference values shift by at most 12% under alternative harmonization parameters. A simple identity links personal use to grid load: E watt-hours per person per day across one billion people corresponds to an average draw of E/24 gigawatts. Data and code are released at https://github.com/AraoufBh/tokwatt, and an online calculator at https://araoufbh.github.io/tokwatt/.

items.title: Toward Human–AI Complementarity in Planning Education: Observations from China
items.abstract: Planning education in China faces cognitive overload, resource inequality, and limited personalized practice. This paper proposes a New Educational Technology System (NETS) that reallocates pedagogical labor between artificial intelligence (AI) and human intelligence based on comparative cognitive advantage. We validate NETS through the Virtual Teaching and Research Section for Territorial Spatial Planning (VTRS-TSP), a consortium of seventy-three Chinese universities. Using mixed methods, including student surveys and instructor interviews, we find that AI-augmented workflows significantly improve efficiency and interdisciplinary knowledge synthesis while preserving human primacy in creative and ethical deliberation. NETS offers a scalable, transferable framework for human-AI complementarity in planning education.

items.title: Towards Elastic Least Privilege for Agent Planning
items.abstract: General-purpose AI agents require authority that changes between tasks and during execution. Common deployments trade broad permissions that expose unnecessary authority and narrow permissions that raise approval requests. Existing mechanisms can enforce dynamic authority, but agent tool interfaces rarely provide the agent's planner, the component that chooses its actions, a means of comparing the authority required by alternative actions or of seeing the cost of the authority it already holds. Drawing on the rich history of access control research, we propose the concept of \emph{elastic least privilege}, in which an agent begins with a small baseline of authority and may acquire more within an owner-defined envelope. Elevations are leased and measured against a replenishing budget. Their cost increases with power, proximity to mandatory safety invariants, and repeated requests. Costs are visible to the planner, which can prefer lower-privilege choices and release authority it no longer needs. Authority returns automatically to the baseline when a lease expires, when it is released, or when the budget is exhausted, while persistent legitimate demand may prompt an owner-approved change to the baseline. Building on prior risk-priced and budget-aware access control, we redesign these mechanisms for agents. How best to implement the approach and how well it works in practice are open research questions. In this paper, we present how the approach could work, illustrate the model, and set an open research agenda.

items.title: Towards fNIRS foundation models: A curated corpus of 67 public datasets with channel positions in MNI space
items.abstract: Brain foundation models have transformed medical artificial intelligence and computational neuroscience by reducing the reliance on task-specific data through large-scale pretraining. While they have been successful with non-invasive neuroimaging data, their adoption in functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has lagged due to the limited size and heterogeneity of public datasets, which are collected under varying protocols, devices, and sensor configurations. In addition, no single fNIRS dataset is comparable in size to the largest datasets in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), or magnetoencephalography (MEG). The fNIRS datasets are also spread across different platforms and often have insufficient information, or lack the protocols that would make them easier to use. Given the advances in EEG foundation models that enable flexible modeling across diverse EEG montages, we curated 1,955 hours of fNIRS data from 67 public datasets spanning 2,798 participants, representing the largest fNIRS curation effort to date. The curated data include oxygenated (HbO) and deoxygenated (HbR) hemoglobin signals along with the three-dimensional position of every channel in the standard space of the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI), which makes positions comparable across datasets. We release dataloaders that handle each dataset automatically, along with the minimal preprocessing pipeline used to prepare the data, at https://github.com/sposso/fnirs-datasets. This work aims to facilitate the future development of foundation models for fNIRS.

items.title: Towards Full-Text Scholarly Argument Mining using Entity-Anchored Claim Extraction
items.abstract: Argument mining in full-text scholarly articles remains an important yet challenging task. This difficulty stems not only from the need to model long-distance dependencies but also from the substantial effort required to annotate sentence-level argumentative components throughout lengthy documents. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach that leverages scientific entity mentions (e.g., tasks, datasets, and models) to identify and structure claims in scholarly literature. We validate our approach through a case study involving 50 full-text research papers on sentiment analysis. We first establish a reliable human gold standard (Krippendorff's $α= 0.80$), identifying 113 claim-bearing sentences and extracting 199 structured claim records from 300 candidate sentences. To address the annotation bottleneck, we employ a majority-voting ensemble of large language models (LLMs) to generate a silver-standard dataset comprising 1,487 claims. Encoders fine-tuned exclusively on the silver-standard dataset outperform those trained on a small human-annotated gold-standard dataset and demonstrate strong zero-shot transfer to NLP papers outside the training corpus.

items.title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs
items.abstract: Production large language models sometimes reward-hack, exploiting flaws in how tasks are scored rather than performing the tasks as intended, sometimes in highly sophisticated and adversarial ways. We investigate the motivations driving this behavior in GPT 5.6 Sol, GPT 5.5, and a checkpoint of OpenAI o3 without safety training ("exp-rl-cap-late") by observing model behavior in agentic environments where the grader is leaked. In our environments, the models appear to be score-seeking: trying to score well according to graders that they believe assess their current actions, even at the expense of violating explicit user instructions. They appear to care about score itself rather than its downstream consequences, violating instructions at approximately the same rate whether the score is indicated to be used for training, for evaluation, or not at all. We observe evidence that the more recent models care to some extent about scores that do not assess their own current actions. GPT 5.6 Sol and GPT 5.5 help other agents 24.6 percentage points more often on average when the other agent stands to gain a score of 1 rather than 0 from being helped. However, when grading or monitoring another trajectory, we find models never collude by distorting its score.

items.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
items.abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

items.title: Training–Rollout Mismatch in Low-Precision LLM Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
items.abstract: Low-precision rollouts can reduce the cost of reinforcement learning for large language models, but numerical discrepancies between the sampler and learner can compromise policy optimization. Even with synchronized parameters and identical token histories, the two execution paths may assign different token probabilities, altering gradient estimation and update decisions. This survey examines how training–rollout mismatch arises, propagates through policy optimization, and evolves over training. We develop a component-level taxonomy that organizes existing approaches by intervention target into two complementary families: numerical design, which aligns execution across learner and sampler paths or preserves numerical fidelity and update visibility; and learning under residual mismatch, which corrects gradient estimation or controls policy updates. We compare the mechanisms, information requirements, and residual errors of these interventions to explain their limitations and how they can be combined. We further synthesize measurement practices and experimental evidence across precision regimes, architectures, and training configurations, examining how numerical discrepancies affect optimization stability, policy improvement, and computational cost. We clarify how differences in policy pairs, metric definitions, and training horizons shape the interpretation of reported results. Open challenges include predicting harmful mismatch, reducing mitigation overhead, sustaining policy improvement over longer training, and comparing methods at matched quality or end-to-end cost.

items.title: Translation education in the age of AI: technics, externalized linguistic memory, and attentional governance
items.abstract: This study draws on Bernard Stiegler’s philosophy of technics to explore how AI reshapes the cognitive and pedagogical conditions of translation education in university settings. Moving beyond a view of AI as a supplementary tool, it argues that AI reconfigures the cognitive ecology of translation learning by altering the relationship among internalized knowledge, externalized linguistic memory, and attention. In AI-mediated translation workflows, textual quality alone no longer provides sufficient evidence of learners’ competence or cognitive engagement. The study therefore identifies attentional governance as a central dimension of translation competence, emphasizing how human scrutiny is directed, adjusted, intensified, and justified across such workflows. It further proposes workflow-based assessment that examines prompting, verification, revision, and justification alongside the final text. By framing translation education as a pharmacological practice, the article shows how pedagogical design can manage the benefits and risks of AI while sustaining interpretive agency.

items.title: Trustworthiness, ethics and the crucial role of open-source AI
items.abstract: Abstract As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes “smarter”, it brings forward more fundamental rather than technical problems to solve, entailing legal, ethical or even philosophical questions. In this session, the core issue of AI “alignment” is investigated under the scope of clarifying the boundaries between human and machine responsibilities, especially in the decision-making process within safety-critical applications. The current legislative status is briefly presented, primarily for the EU and USA, regarding “safe” and “trustworthy” AI, while the role of open-source models, platforms and applications is explored as probably the most important aspect. Furthermore, the moral aspects of fully autonomous AI systems are discussed through the classic “trolley problem”, demonstrating the difficulties of even formulating such tasks for designing AI. Finally, ten core principles of “aligned” AI are summarized and a few suggestions are discussed regarding how these principles may be incorporated in practice towards this direction.

items.title: Trustworthy Transfer Learning in GeoAI: Assessing Pretrained Models for Rooftop Solar PV Mapping Under Geographic Domain Shift
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing availability of pretrained Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) models has accelerated the operational adoption of deep learning within geographic information systems. However, models developed in one geographic region frequently experience performance degradation when deployed elsewhere because of geographic domain shift. Although transfer learning is widely used to improve cross-regional model performance, it remains unclear whether improved predictive accuracy alone provides sufficient evidence for trustworthy deployment. This study investigates this question using rooftop solar photovoltaic mapping in Brisbane, Australia, as an operational case study. Esri’s pretrained US Solar Panel Detection model was locally calibrated through transfer learning and evaluated using both development and geographically independent test datasets. Local calibration substantially improved detection performance, increasing recall from 38.5% to 84.1% on the development dataset while maintaining strong performance on the independent test dataset, demonstrating effective adaptation to geographic domain shift. However, independent evaluation and qualitative error analysis also revealed persistent false positives, missed detections, and geometric segmentation errors, indicating that residual uncertainty remained following transfer learning. These findings demonstrate that although transfer learning substantially improves robustness, reliability, and model generalisation, predictive performance alone is insufficient to establish trustworthy deployment. By integrating complementary evidence relating to robustness, reliability, generalisation, transparency, and residual uncertainty, this study provides an operational approach for evaluating the trustworthiness of pretrained GeoAI models prior to deployment in geographically distinct environments.

items.title: Try Before You Evolve: Ranking-Scored Trials for Recursive Self-Improvement of Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Recommenders on Web platforms such as e-commerce and music streaming need their training recipes re-tuned for each dataset. Large language model (LLM) agents can now rewrite these recipes, enabling recursive self-improvement (RSI) of recommender systems. Existing agents propose one edit per round, fully retrain the recommender, and keep the edit only if its ranking quality improves. Unlike programs or patches that can be scored by execution, a recommender edit changes how the model is trained, which raises two challenges. First, ranking feedback is delayed: an edit's ranking quality is known only after full retraining, so much of the retraining budget goes to edits that are later discarded. Second, the signals available before retraining are unreliable: sampled training losses can look solved while full-ranking performance remains poor, and they are not comparable across edits that change the loss or sampler. We propose RecRSI, which generates diverse candidate edits from a diagnosis of the current model and selects one for full retraining using early ranking feedback: each candidate receives a short trial, the first steps of its full training run, scored by full-ranking NDCG@10 on held-out probe users. With two sequential recommenders on three datasets and the same number of full retrainings, RecRSI significantly outperforms existing self-evolving agents in every setting, and on both Amazon datasets reaches in its first round a ranking quality that none of them reaches in five.

items.title: Understanding Older Adults’ Evaluation of AI-Generated Health Information
items.abstract: When older adults cannot distinguish accurate health information from misinformation within AI-generated content, they may misjudge its credibility and follow incorrect advice. To investigate how information characteristics shape older adults’ assessment of AI-generated health content, this study employed a 2 × 2 × 2 within-subject design manipulating emotional framing (fear vs. neutral), authority cues (high vs. low), and information veracity (true vs. false), with individual differences examined as exploratory variables. Seven older adults rated the credibility and adoption intention of AI-generated information and chose whether to verify it. Those verifying viewed corrections and re-rated initial information. Results showed that emotional framing and authority cues impaired participants’ ability to identify misinformation. Individuals with higher digital literacy and cognitive ability relied less on emotional framing. Findings suggest that such information characteristics make misinformation harder to identify, whereas digital literacy and cognitive ability may buffer this effect by reducing reliance on them.

items.title: Understanding the drivers and barriers of human–AI knowledge orchestration: insights from social exchange theory
items.abstract: Purpose Despite the application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in organizational workflows and business processes, many firms have not achieved improvements in innovation capabilities and value creation. This suggests that capability development depends not only on artificial intelligence (AI) but also on the effective orchestration human and artificial knowledge in work routines and business activities. This study explores the mechanisms underlying human–AI knowledge orchestration (KO) and identifies drivers, inhibitors and boundary conditions shaping managers’ participation. Design/methodology/approach Integrating knowledge orchestration theory and social exchange theory, the study conceptualizes knowledge growth, AI self-efficacy (AISE), perceived organizational support as benefits, execution cost (EC) and knowledge power loss as costs and trust in AI as the moderator. The model is tested using structural equation model with data from 341 managers in AI adopting firms. Findings Knowledge growth, AISE and perceived organizational support positively affect human–AI KO, whereas EC and loss of knowledge power (LKP) have negative impact. Trust in AI strengthens the positive effect of knowledge growth and AISE but unexpectedly exacerbates negative impact of EC and LKP. Social implications This study highlights the importance of fostering trust and addressing barriers in human–AI collaboration, offering insights into the responsible adoption of AI in the workplace. The findings may contribute to more inclusive digital transformation and AI-enabled knowledge management practices. Originality/value By conceptualizing human–AI KO as a dynamic knowledge management process embedded in workflows and business processes, this study advances research at the intersection of AI, knowledge management and business process management. It responds to calls to embed knowledge management in work routines and examine individual-level factors in AI-supported business processes. It reveals the benefit–cost trade-off underlying managers’ participation and provides implications for AI-enabled knowledge management, business process improvement and capability development.

items.title: UniffordInteractor: Reasoning the Unified Affordance for Human and Multi-Object Interaction
items.abstract: Deriving plausible and dynamic Human Object Interaction (HOI) has gained tremendous progress in Embodied AI and Immersive AR/VR. While existing HOI methods have effectively explored human interaction with individual or fixed objects, they still show limitations in complex multi-object interaction scenes. Meanwhile, previous approaches focus more on the contact information held by human-object relation, overlooking the significance of the contact situation of various entities (i.e., object-object). To address these limitations, we propose UniffordInteractor, a Reasoning-then-Interacting framework that leverages unified affordance for realistic and long-horizon human and multi-object interaction modeling. At the reasoning stage, we devise a Unified Affordance Reasoner (UAR) that employs a fine-tuned 3D Multimodal Large Language Model for unified object-centric affordance prediction. At the interacting stage, we propose Hierarchical Interaction Generator (HIG), which formulates the interaction generation as a hierarchical (e.g., root to body to hand to objects) autoregressive prediction, conditioned on the obtained unified affordance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniffordInteractor surpasses SOTA counterparts in human and multi-object interaction generation.

items.title: Unpacking AI Service and Customer Engagement in Indonesian Retail: The Mediating Role of Intention and The Moderating Role of Trust
items.abstract: This study investigates the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) service on customer engagement in the Indonesian retail industry, with intention as a mediator and trust as a moderator. A quantitative research design was employed using Structural Equation Modelling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS), with data collected from retail customers across Indonesia who had experience using AI-based services such as chatbots, recommendation systems, and virtual assistants. The findings reveal a significant positive impact of AI service on customer engagement (p < 0.001). Furthermore, intention played a significant mediating role between AI service and customer engagement (p < 0.001), supporting the Theory of Planned Behaviour. Contrary to theoretical expectations, trust was not a significant moderator between AI service and intention (p = 0.331), nor between intention and customer engagement (p = 0.337). The proposed model explained 43% of the variance in customer engagement and 49% of the variance in intention, indicating moderate predictive power. The non-significant moderating role of trust suggests that Indonesian consumers may have developed high trust in digital technologies due to the rapid growth of e-commerce and digital financial services, or that the utilitarian nature of AI services reduces the salience of trust as a boundary condition. These findings offer both theoretical and practical implications regarding the implementation of AI service. Theoretically, the study extends the Theory of Planned Behaviour to AI service adoption in emerging economies and questions trust's generalizability as a moderator. Practically, retailers should invest in AI capabilities and foster positive customer intentions.

items.title: Unstable witnessing: war images and the crisis of perception in the age of generative AI
items.abstract: This article examines how the coexistence of photographic and AI-generated war imagery reconfigures the conditions of media witnessing (Frosh and Pinchevski 2009). Today’s platformed visual culture is characterized not only by an unprecedented abundance of images, but also by the convergence of images produced through fundamentally different operations: whereas traditional photography registers light from scenes before a camera, generative AI models synthesize photographic-looking images through statistical prediction. Thus, photorealism (Hausken 2024) no longer guarantees indexical registrations of the world. Through reception-oriented analysis of Thomas Hirschhorn’s Pixel-Collages (2015–2016) and Ilkin Huseynov’s Looming Dreams (2023), the article traces how this transformation becomes perceptible in contemporary art. Hirschhorn’s collages engage with poor images (Steyerl 2013a): traditionally produced photographs whose evidentiary meanings are destabilized through postproduction, recirculation, and decontextualization. Huseynov’s AI-generated images, by contrast, depict war without detecting particular events, nevertheless retaining a genealogical relation to photography through their training data and the reproduction of the photographic form. Read sequentially, the works demonstrate that epistemic uncertainty (Chouliaraki 2015) spans rather than separates photographic and synthetic imagery: photographic registration cannot guarantee stable meaning-making, while photographic appearance no longer guarantees that registration even occurred. Bringing Wolfgang Welsch’s concept of derealization into dialogue with theories of new media, centrally the concept of digital witnessing Chouliaraki 2015) and secondary witnessing (Varvia 2024), the article develops the concept of unstable witnessing. This describes a mode of reception in which images remain indispensable to sensing and perceiving distant wars, while intensified exposure and heterogeneous modes of image production make their provenance and evidentiary status increasingly difficult to establish. The artworks do not resolve this uncertainty but render its perceptual operations visible, staging contemporary media witnessing as suspended between trust and distrust, testimony and fabrication, and sense-making and its breakdown.

items.title: UPPAAi: Towards LLM-Assisted Modeling, Verification, Analysis and Synthesis
items.abstract: For more than three decades, UPPAAL has supported the modelling and analysis of real-time and cyber-physical systems. Yet building a suitable model, formalising the intended properties, choosing analysis techniques and interpreting counterexamples remain iterative tasks that demand substantial expertise. Large language models (LLMs) can offer plausible explanations and even solutions, but they are not necessarily correct. We present UPPAAI, an extension of UPPAAL in which users construct, explain, debug and specify models in dialogue with an LLM. The guiding principle is that the user requests, the LLM proposes, explains and orchestrates, and UPPAAL verifies. UPPAAI exposes the UPPAAL editor, queries and verifier through a Tools API. We report on seven case studies, from explaining to a newcomer to learning a controller, covering timed automata, stochastic hybrid automata and strategy learning. LLMs proved to be extremely helpful in not just generating solutions but also pro-actively suggesting relevant UPPAAL features it was not asked about.
